content_voiceover: Here's the core intravascular fibrinolysis pathway, so let's trace it step by step. On the right side, thrombin, labeled IIa, converts fibrinogen into crosslinked fibrin, that's the clot-forming side you already know. On the left side, t-PA, tissue-type plasminogen activator, converts plasminogen into plasmin. Plasmin is the active enzyme that then acts directly on the crosslinked fibrin, driving fibrin clot dissolution, shown at the bottom. So in a single glance, you have the whole loop: thrombin builds the fibrin clot, while t-PA activated plasmin tears it back down. Both processes are happening in the same vascular space, and their relative activity determines whether a clot grows, stabilizes, or resolves.
keypoints: t-PA converts plasminogen into active plasmin
Thrombin, factor IIa, converts fibrinogen into crosslinked fibrin
Net effect is fibrin clot dissolution
keypoint_voiceover: In short, t-PA activates plasminogen into plasmin, thrombin builds crosslinked fibrin from fibrinogen, and plasmin then dissolves that crosslinked fibrin, completing the balance between clot formation and clot breakdown.
